title: Natural and Made Materials
seo_title: Year 4 Science: Natural and Made Materials Worksheets (Australian Curriculum)
standard_text: Compare the properties of natural and made materials and relate their properties to their uses, including materials used by First Nations Australians (summary of the Australian Curriculum v9.0 Science content description).
meta_desc: Free Year 4 science worksheets on natural and made materials: where materials come from, their properties, and choosing the best material for a job. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Choose a material by its properties.
key_sub: Natural materials come from nature; made materials are changed by people.
body_html:
How to think about it

Materials can be natural or made (processed).

  • Natural materials are found in nature: wood, wool, cotton, stone, clay, bark.
  • Made materials are made by people from natural ones: glass from sand, paper from wood, plastic from oil, bricks from clay.
  • We choose a material by its properties: strong, flexible, waterproof, transparent, hard, absorbent or a good insulator.
Example

Is glass natural or made?

it is made by heating sand

Answer: made

Example

Best material for a raincoat?

it must keep water out

Answer: a waterproof material such as plastic

Common mistakes

  • Thinking paper or glass are natural because they come from natural things.
  • Choosing a material by colour instead of its properties.
  • Thinking made materials are always better than natural ones.

faq.q: What is the difference between natural and made materials?
faq.a: Natural materials, such as wood and wool, come from nature. Made materials, such as plastic and glass, are made by people by changing natural materials.

faq.q: How do we choose the best material?
faq.a: Think about the job, then choose the properties it needs: for example, waterproof for a raincoat or transparent for a window.

faq.q: Which natural materials did First Nations Australians use?
faq.a: They used bark for canoes and shelters, stone for tools, wood for spears and shields, and plant resins such as spinifex resin as glue.
